title: UPDATE: DeepSeek and MiniMax Receive Overseas Licenses Ahead of China's AI Export Controls
summary:
Chinese AI developers DeepSeek and MiniMax have received licenses for overseas use, according to Chinese media, as Beijing implements interim registration requirements ahead of broader technology export controls. The Ministry of Commerce also announced optimized screening and identification procedures for dual-use export controls that take effect Nov. 18, following public consultations on the draft rules closing Nov. 15.

The draft export catalogue adds 40 technologies across artificial intelligence, solar manufacturing and biotechnology, banning 14 items and restricting 26. The 23 AI entries require government approval to transfer overseas the weights, checkpoints or source code of models with at least 2T parameters, training compute of at least 10^26 operations, or a global top 10 ranking in performance, usage, safety or training efficiency. The proposal also bans exports of models trained on national core data and AI systems that autonomously generate malware beating mainstream antivirus software at least 85% of the time or rewrite at least 50% of their code per execution.

While deploying restricted models on foreign servers requires a license, the commerce ministry clarified that API access, web and app interfaces, software-as-a-service and lightweight on-device deployments do not count as large-model technology exports. Models already in the public domain through open-source release or academic papers are exempt, and Beijing said new open-source releases, overseas chip tape-outs and foreign computing centers operated by Chinese firms will qualify for automatic licensing to proceed upon filing.

selectedTweets.text: This move does not mean “China is shutting down open-weight models,” but it does indicate the Chinese government establishing the optionality to shut down future open-weight models at will. It’s also a mirror image of the model-weight export control regime USG has already used.
selectedTweets.quotedTweetText:
HOLY. China is moving to put 23 AI technologies under export controls, including large models, AI agents and computing clusters, as part of a sweeping proposal to ban exports of 14 technologies and restrict another 26.

The rules would ban technology for AI systems that autonomously generate or mutate malware, while AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and overseas deployment of restricted Chinese models would require approval.

APIs, apps, SaaS and already-public open-source technologies are exempt.

Exporters must begin registering covered overseas technology transfers today, before the final controls are adopted. Public consultation closes November 15.

selectedTweets.text:
My initial reaction to China's new AI export controls:

They're confusing because they seem to be creating restrictions for China AI exports while simultaneously signaling continued "automatic" approval for open-source models.

I don't think it's about leverage. I think China is generally worried about cyberattack potential for Chinese AI systems and don't want these proliferating outside China and then potentially hitting Chinese critical infrastructure or government systems.

So the toughest restrictions--the prohibitions 禁止出口--are on AI autonomous malicious code generation. But there are also broad restrictions 限制出口 on AI models of above certain performance thresholds. Ministry of Commerce later said open-source models would be "automatically" approved upon registration, but then it does lay the groundwork for a more systematic monitoring of models and possible real restrictions later on.

The part that's confusing to me is that AI systems that can help produce malware basically include all the top Chinese open-source models. And yet they're simultaneously "automatically" approved?

It seems like this set of new export controls were created by one part of the bureaucracy that's worried about proliferation of harmful AI capabilities but then another part is trying to say "but actually we still support open-source."

This is at least my initial reaction--my views may change as I re-read and re-analyze.

selectedTweets.quotedTweetText:
Beijing just took a big step towards closing the Chinese frontier. The rules could give China's government the power to restrict AI developers from releasing their most advanced open-weight models.

It proposes banning exports of AI technologies that autonomously generate and modify malicious code. It also wants to restrict exports of AI-assisted vulnerability-discovery technologies. Giving a model away for free, ie open-weight, could qualify as an export.

Crucially, the rules distinguish between technologies already in the public domain and those not yet released. It specifically exempts existing open-source models. But new releases could potentially trigger export controls.

Providing foreign customers with access to models through APIs (ie, closed models) is generally exempt, whereas restricted models being served overseas could require a licence.

Beijing promises essentially automatic licensing for open-source releases, allowing developers to publish almost immediately after notification. But it's unclear whether this applies to those capabilities proposed for outright export prohibition. 

If intelligence generalises, how can China's AI labs distinguish between a smart model and one that has the capabilities proposes for restrictions?

selectedTweets.text:
China wants to put AI models on its export control list.

Reuters, today: 40 technologies, 23 of them AI. Models, agents, compute clusters. Registration starts now, final rules after 15 Nov.

My feed in 1 hour: "Chinese open weights are dead."

Then I read the Ministry of Commerce Q&A.

Already open sourced or published in papers: not covered.
Open sourcing new AI tech: "automatic license".
API, apps, SaaS, small on-device models: not export at all.
Deploying a restricted model on servers abroad: export.

So the models I run at home are fine. Today.

But an automatic license is still a license. Today Beijing signs it automatically. Tomorrow it can stop signing.

I see it like this. The best thing China gave the world this year was weights you can download. If the next Qwen Max or Kimi goes API only because of a list, China copies the worst thing OpenAI ever did.

Comments are open until 15 Nov. I hope every Chinese lab that ships weights sends one.

selectedTweets.text:
Really important update from China's ministry of commerce and ministry of science and tech (h/t @Nectar_Gan), not because it signals that the government's honeymoon period with open weight AI is over, far from it. But because it further confirms that as China's working on building out a more robust AI risk management regime (sth discussed in this year's Five Year Plan, see photo below, & by Xi at the World of AI Conference), it is singling out high-risk open models for more scrutiny. It appears that if the risks/ capabilities demand, a filing regime or prohibition may be considered, but this will be narrowly enforced and affect only a small number of products & services. 

So, what hasn't changed: Open model releases at home and abroad remain a welcomed development by the government. 

What has been clarified: On the open weight AI front, expect China to step up capability/risk-based governance to meet domestic needs, global demands. 

Here are the relevant discussions and sentences (I'll let X's translate function do its job):
1. 此次修订亦是技术贸易管理的**常态化⼯作**，依法依规进⾏，不针对任何特定国家、地区或实体。
2. 近年来，⼈⼯智能、⽣物医药和光伏相关技术在敏感领域的应⽤不断拓展，各主要经济体均实施了不同程度的出⼝管控。
3. 中国参考国际通⾏做法，依法实施必要的管理，既**防范技术失控和不当扩散⻛险，也保障正常国际技术交流合作**，推动科技向上向善、安全可控、造福⼈类。
4. 中国政府⼀贯⽀持企业依法依规开展互利共赢的跨国经营与国际技术合作，**有关政策⽴场没有改变**。
5. 此次拟将⼈⼯智能⼤模型、智能体、⼒集群、信息处理相关23项关键技术增列⾄《⽬录》，主要有以下考虑：... 此次拟列管的**⼈⼯智能⾃主驱动恶意代码⽣成与变异技术等，可被⽤于攻击国家关键信息基础设施、国防军⼯、核
⼼政务等敏感系统，或⽤于绕过国家安全防御体系**。
6. ⿎励开源开放、合作共享。... **为⽀持构建⼈⼯智能开源创新⽣态体系，对⼈⼯智能类技术开源、中国企业在境外⾃建⾃营算⼒中⼼、赴境外开展芯⽚流⽚制造、利⽤境外资源开展联合研发、参与国际标准制定等情形的技术出，适⽤⾃动许可等便利措施，基本实现“即报即出”** ；对已通过开源、发表学术论⽂等⽅式进⼊公共领域的相关技术，拟不纳⼊出⼝管理范围，为⼈⼯智能技术国际交流合作创造良好环。
7. 需要特别指出的是，中⽅主张在相互尊重、平等互利基础上，与各国开展⼈⼯智能对话合作，**共同应对⼈⼯智能技术扩散和失控⻛险**。
8. **有关措施正式实施后，绝⼤部分⼈⼯智能技术仍可以⾃由出⼝。** 对于纳⼊限制类的⼈⼯智能技术，开展海外本地化部署，属于技术出⼝管理范围；**如果部署在海外⾃有云等⻛险相对可控的情形下，可适⽤⾃动许可等便利措施。** 对于企业利⽤限制类⼤模型对外提供API调⽤、APP/⽹⻚交互、SaaS应⽤、本地端侧轻量化部署等情形，不属于⼤模型技术出⼝管理范围。
(highlights are mine)

Overall, this doc does not strike me as a trade bargaining chip as much as primarily an AI security play & secondarily a soft power play (i.e. responding to global concerns over risks from frontier open models). This development/ document also chimes with my predictions back in July https://t.co/qSXWvZx7lj & my observations last month: https://t.co/WoHpqyH9hB.
